2003.title: Kal Ho Naa Ho
2003.note: Nikhil Advani's Kal Ho Naa Ho is the film that solidified the New York NRI diaspora as Hindi cinema's emotional heartland, a move that brought the industry enormous overseas revenue and shaped its aesthetic for most of the decade. Shah Rukh Khan playing a dying man who orchestrates love for someone else is the film's most counterintuitive and effective choice. Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy's score, particularly the title track, is among the decade's most emotionally precise compositions.

2003.title: Koi... Mil Gaya
2003.note: Rakesh Roshan's Koi Mil Gaya is a genuinely unusual film — an alien contact story set in a small Indian town, anchored by a mentally challenged protagonist, that managed to be simultaneously scientifically absurd and emotionally sincere. Hrithik Roshan's performance as Rohit, requiring him to inhabit a childlike innocence without condescension, is one of the most technically demanding things he has done. The franchise it launched — Krrish — is Indian cinema's most sustained superhero universe.

2003.title: Main Hoon Na
2003.note: Farah Khan's debut film is a love letter to 1970s Bollywood — its conventions, its music, its emotional excess — made by someone who understood those conventions from the inside and reproduced them with affection rather than irony. Shah Rukh Khan playing both an undercover soldier and a student is a dual register the film handles by simply making the campus sequences more fun than the action ones. The film's complete sincerity is what distinguishes it from the parody it could easily have become.

2003.title: Baghban
2003.note: Ravi Chopra's Baghban hit a nerve that most Hindi films of the era carefully avoided — the specific loneliness of ageing parents in a society that has imported Western individualism without maintaining the traditional structures of care. Amitabh Bachchan and Hema Malini's performances are the film's entire argument: that this loneliness is real, specific, and visible. The film played in single screens to audiences who were simultaneously watching it and living it.

2003.title: Tere Naam
2003.note: Satish Kaushik's Tere Naam gave Salman Khan his most unhinged and compelling dramatic performance — a man whose love becomes obsession and whose obsession becomes psychosis, a character arc the film does not flinch from. The hairstyle became a pan-Indian craze almost immediately, which is interesting given how dark the character wearing it actually is. The film's Tamil Nadu performance, where it ran for months in dubbed version, demonstrated the emerging pan-India appetite for this kind of intense romantic drama.

2003.title: Ishq Vishk
2003.note: Ken Ghosh's Ishq Vishk is the film that introduced Shahid Kapoor and marked a specific moment in Hindi romantic cinema — the gentle, boyish lead who wins through charm rather than alpha assertion. Amrita Rao and Shenaz Treasury as the two love interests gave the film a textural lightness that matched Kapoor's debut register. The film launched a career that would eventually find more dramatically interesting territory.

2003.title: Oke Okkadu
2003.note: Vikram K. Kumar's Oke Okkadu is a Telugu remake of Minnale that gave Arjun Sarja's daughter Aishwarya a lead role and Mahesh Babu's brother Naresh a brief mainstream moment. The film's real significance is as a marker of how efficiently Telugu cinema was adapting successful Tamil templates during this period.

2003.title: Boys
2003.note: Shankar's Boys is the Tamil director's least characteristically Shankar film — a youth ensemble about friendship, ambition and a rock band that operates in a lighter register than his usual maximalism. The film gave AR Rahman one of his most playful scores, and the ensemble of young actors generated an energy that Shankar's more star-dependent productions sometimes lack. A film about the texture of being young rather than about ideas.

2003.title: Ghilli
2003.note: Dharani's Ghilli — a remake of Telugu Okkadu — is Vijay's commercial coronation in Tamil cinema, the film that converted his considerable popularity into undisputed star status. The action-romance hybrid gave him both registers simultaneously and demonstrated that he could carry both without either diminishing the other. AR Rahman's 'Appadi Podu' became one of Tamil cinema's most replayed song sequences.

2003.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
2003.note: Peter Jackson's Return of the King completed the most ambitious film trilogy ever attempted and found in India a substantial audience that had followed all three films across three years — a commitment that the pre-streaming era required genuine dedication. The film's Academy dominance (eleven Oscars) was widely covered in Indian entertainment media, elevating Hollywood prestige cinema's profile with the urban audience.

2003.title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl

2004.title: Veer-Zaara
2004.note: Yash Chopra's final directorial film is a willed act of optimism about India-Pakistan relations made in the language of romantic mythologisation — two countries as two lovers separated by politics, held apart by duty, reunited after decades by persistence. Shah Rukh Khan and Preity Zinta achieve a tenderness that transcends the film's melodramatic architecture. The film's box office performance confirmed that there was still a large audience for old-fashioned romantic sincerity.

2004.title: Dhoom
2004.note: Sanjay Gadhvi's Dhoom established the motorcycle action film as a sustainable Hindi cinema genre and launched the decade's most reliable franchise. Abhishek Bachchan and Uday Chopra as the cop duo provided the straight-man framework against which each film's villain — John Abraham here, then Hrithik Roshan, then Aamir Khan — could operate. John Abraham's physicality and the bike sequences gave Indian action cinema a kinetic vocabulary it had been searching for.

2004.title: Hum Tum
2004.note: Kunal Kohli's Hum Tum is the most emotionally intelligent romantic comedy Hindi cinema produced in the mid-2000s — Saif Ali Khan and Rani Mukerji across multiple meetings and stages of life, the film's episodic structure allowing it to be honest about how people change. The film's mature treatment of divorce and loss within an otherwise light register was genuinely unusual. Saif Ali Khan's comic timing reached its commercial peak here.

2004.title: Murder
2004.note: Anurag Basu's Murder introduced Mallika Sherawat to the mainstream through a thriller that used adult content more explicitly than Hindi cinema's contemporary mainstream generally permitted. The film's commercial success created a template for the Bhatt camp's adult thriller formula that would generate multiple sequels. Emraan Hashmi's serial-kisser identity was a direct product of this film.

2004.title: Swades
2004.note: Ashutosh Gowariker's Swades is among the most intellectually serious popular films in Hindi cinema — a development worker returning from NASA to his village in Rajasthan, confronting what India actually is rather than what nostalgia suggests it should be. Shah Rukh Khan's Mohan Bhargava is the character that asks the most of him dramatically, requiring him to inhabit a quietness his stardom rarely permits. The film's commercial failure and critical respect sit in a productive tension that defines a specific type of ambitious Indian filmmaking.

2004.title: Aparichitudu
2004.note: Linguswamy's Aparichitudu is the Telugu remake of Anniyan that gave Vikram's multiple-personality thriller a language and market extension. The two versions' simultaneous existence demonstrated how fluidly successful concepts moved between Indian language industries during this period, and how differently the same character can read across cultural contexts.

2004.title: Anniyan
2004.note: Shankar's Anniyan is the most cinematically extravagant exploration of multiple personality disorder that Indian cinema has produced — a legal-thriller-fantasy-action hybrid that uses Vikram's extraordinary physical transformation ability to argue something genuinely interesting about social compliance and its psychological cost. The three personalities require three entirely different performance registers, and Vikram moves between them with a fluency that is technically astonishing. The film's ₹70 Cr collection made it Tamil cinema's highest-grossing release to that point.

2004.title: Chandramukhi
2004.note: P. Vasu's Chandramukhi gave Rajinikanth a vehicle perfectly calibrated to his specific performance gifts — comedy, action, and a climactic revelation that requires him to inhabit a supernatural authority the camera instantly accepts. Jyothika's dual performance as the modern woman and the classical dancer is the film's actual structural achievement, though the marketing — inevitably — foregrounded Rajinikanth. The film held the Tamil Nadu box office record for several years.

2004.title: Autograph
2004.note: Cheran's Autograph is one of Tamil cinema's most delicately constructed romantic films — an episodic story structured around a man's memories of the women who shaped his life before his wedding. The film's emotional intelligence and its willingness to let scenes breathe without conventional dramatic acceleration made it a significant departure from Tamil commercial cinema's usual tempo.

2004.title: Apthamitra
2004.note: P. Vasu's Apthamitra was Kannada cinema's biggest commercial hit of the era and remains one of the most technically ambitious horror films produced in Indian regional language cinema. Ramesh Aravind's protagonist and the supernatural premise gave the film a genre credibility that Kannada commercial cinema had rarely attempted. Its success created space for more genre experimentation in Sandalwood.

2004.title: Mungaru Male
2004.note: Yogaraj Bhat's Mungaru Male was the commercial breakthrough that made Kannada cinema's existence as a viable mainstream industry undeniable — ₹40 Cr in a relatively small market, running for over a year. Ganesh and Pooja Gandhi's performances grounded the romantic rain sequences in an emotional sincerity that the film's enormous musical popularity sometimes obscures. The film's satellite rights sold at a price that reoriented how Kannada producers thought about their market.

2004.title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban

2005.title: No Entry
2005.note: Anees Bazmee's No Entry is the most efficiently assembled Hindi ensemble comedy of the decade — a film about three men trying to have affairs and spectacularly failing, constructed around the specific comic strengths of Salman Khan, Anil Kapoor and Fardeen Khan. The script's mechanism is precise: escalating complications managed with a timing that the ensemble honours completely. The film ran for months on the strength of its first-week audience telling everyone else to go.

2005.title: Bunty Aur Babli
2005.note: Shaad Ali's Bunty Aur Babli is the most fun Hindi film of 2005 — Abhishek Bachchan and Rani Mukerji as two small-town dreamers who become con artists, a premise Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy's score transforms into a road movie of constant buoyancy. The 'Kajra Re' sequence, an item number parachuted into the film with no justification beyond sheer pleasure, became the year's most replayed musical moment. Amitabh Bachchan's supporting turn as the cop pursuing them is quietly one of his best performances of the decade.

2005.title: Black
2005.note: Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Black is the most formally ambitious film of his career — a story of a deaf-blind woman and her teacher, told without the narrative shortcuts that the subject might have tempted a lesser director to use. Amitabh Bachchan and Rani Mukerji both give performances of extraordinary physical and emotional precision, and Bhansali's visual grammar — snow, glass, silence — creates a world whose conditions the audience genuinely inhabits. A film that deserved every award it received.

2005.title: Salaam Namaste
2005.note: Siddharth Anand's Salaam Namaste was the first mainstream Hindi film to treat live-in relationships as a straightforward romantic premise rather than a social problem, and the Pune NRI-adjacent setting gave it a cosmopolitan permission to do so. Saif Ali Khan and Preity Zinta generate an easy, bickering chemistry that the film's eventual pregnancy storyline tests rather than resolves neatly. The film's commercial success was a genuine signal about how the urban audience's values were shifting.

2005.title: Bluffmaster!
2005.note: Rohan Sippy's Bluffmaster! is the most visually stylish con-artist film in Hindi cinema — a Mumbai heist caper with Abhishek Bachchan and Priyanka Chopra that drew on Tarantino's structural grammar without becoming a pastiche. The film's Vishal-Shekhar score, particularly 'Right Here Right Now', gave the decade a genuinely contemporary sound. Among the more formally adventurous mainstream films of 2005.

2005.title: Sarkar
2005.note: Ram Gopal Varma's Sarkar — his Godfather — gave Amitabh Bachchan a performance context that positioned his age and gravity as assets rather than limitations. The film's visual language is among Varma's most controlled, and the father-son dynamic between Bachchan and Abhishek Bachchan generates an offscreen resonance that the film acknowledges without exploiting. Among the most formally serious Hindi films of 2005.

2005.title: Pokiri
2005.note: Puri Jagannadh's Pokiri gave Mahesh Babu his largest commercial success to that point and established the undercover-cop-as-gangster formula that Telugu cinema would rework repeatedly across the following decade. The film's action sequences are constructed with a technical ambition unusual for Telugu commercial cinema of 2005, and Mahesh Babu's physical credibility in those sequences resolved any lingering uncertainty about his action star potential. The Hindi remake, Wanted, was Salman Khan's commercial comeback vehicle.

2005.title: Chatrapathi
2005.note: S.S. Rajamouli's Chatrapathi is a Telugu action film that demonstrates how completely Rajamouli had absorbed the grammar of mass commercial cinema — a refugee protagonist fighting for dignity and survival that gave Prabhas his most commercially significant early role. The film's action sequences show Rajamouli refining the visual language of large-scale Telugu action that would reach its pinnacle in Baahubali.

2005.title: Poi
2005.note: Selvaraghavan's Poi is a Tamil psychological thriller about obsession and deception that operates in the director's characteristic mode of making audiences uncomfortable with their own sympathies. The film's portrait of a controlling relationship — who is being controlled, who is controlling whom — resists easy resolution in ways that mainstream Tamil cinema rarely permits.

2005.title: Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire

2006.title: Dhoom 2
2006.note: Sanjay Gadhvi's Dhoom 2 elevated the franchise from an efficient action entertainment to a genuine spectacle — primarily through casting Hrithik Roshan as the villain, a decision that rebalanced the entire film's moral and aesthetic gravity. The opening sequence, a train heist in the African desert, announced the film's ambitions immediately. Ash and Hrithik's chemistry generated a specific kind of visual electricity that Bollywood's marketing machinery recognised and maximised.

2006.title: Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna
2006.note: Karan Johar's Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna is Hindi cinema's most serious engagement with adult marital dissatisfaction — a film about two unhappily married people falling in love with each other, made by a director with the commercial infrastructure to give the subject a wide release. Its India reception was more cautious than its overseas performance, which confirmed a thesis the film was almost certainly exploring: that the diaspora had processed these questions more completely than the domestic audience. A film that is more interesting than its controversy suggests.

2006.title: Lage Raho Munna Bhai
2006.note: Rajkumar Hirani's sequel is the rarest thing in Indian cinema — a follow-up that surpassed the original by asking a more interesting question. Making Gandhi not a historical icon but a living presence who advises a gangster on nonviolence required the kind of conceptual courage that mainstream Indian cinema almost never musters. The film's 'Gandhigiri' entered common usage immediately, and Hirani's ability to deliver social philosophy in the language of entertainment has never been more precisely demonstrated.

2006.title: Don
2006.note: Farhan Akhtar's Don remake took the 1978 Amitabh Bachchan classic and rebuilt it entirely from tone and structure — darker, sleeker, operating in a post-Matrix visual register that the 2006 audience was ready for. Shah Rukh Khan understood that he was not replacing Bachchan but occupying the same structural space with a different performance vocabulary, and the restraint of that understanding produced one of his finest non-romantic performances. The film left its ending deliberately unresolved, a conceptual choice that was rewarded commercially.

2006.title: Rang De Basanti
2006.note: Rakeysh Omprakash Mehra's Rang De Basanti is the film that made the Indian urban middle class believe, briefly and intensely, that political engagement was possible and meaningful. The structural device — contemporary youth inhabiting the spirits of freedom fighters — is conceptually elegant and emotionally devastating in execution. The film's final act, which converts the narrative's optimism into a specific kind of political violence, is one of Hindi cinema's most genuinely challenging endings.

2006.title: Fanaa
2006.note: Kunal Kohli's Fanaa is built on its central plot reversal — the romantic lead revealed as a terrorist — and Aamir Khan's willingness to let the film's second half make his character genuinely frightening is the performance choice that distinguishes it from a conventional romance. Kajol's return to the screen after a five-year gap gave the film its emotional anchor. The film's Kashmir setting and terrorist premise generated political controversy that the box office absorbed without apparent damage.

2006.title: Vivah
2006.note: Sooraj Barjatya's Vivah is the most commercially successful defence of traditional values in 2000s Hindi cinema — a film that treats arranged marriage, family obligation and domestic virtue as genuinely aspirational. The film's massive collection came from exactly the audience that Bollywood's urban, cosmopolitan turn had begun to leave behind. Shahid Kapoor and Amrita Rao's restrained performances gave the film a sincerity that its ideology, regardless of one's agreement with it, cannot be denied.

2006.title: Omkara
2006.note: Vishal Bhardwaj's Omkara — his Othello — is the finest Shakespeare adaptation in Hindi cinema, a film that translates the play's jealousy and betrayal into Uttar Pradesh's political criminality with a fidelity to the original's darkness that Indian mainstream cinema almost never permits. Saif Ali Khan's Langda Tyagi is one of the decade's great villain performances, and Ajay Devgn's Omkara carries an authority earned through physicality rather than declared through dialogue. A film that required a serious audience and found one.

2006.title: Bommarillu
2006.note: Bhaskar's Bommarillu is one of Telugu cinema's most emotionally precise family films — a story about a son's relationship with his overprotective father that treats both positions with genuine understanding rather than sitcom simplification. Siddharth's performance carries the film's central conflict with a spontaneity that the dialogue's quality alone couldn't achieve. Devi Sri Prasad's score gave Telugu romantic cinema a new sonic template.

2006.title: Vikramarkudu
2006.note: S.S. Rajamouli's Vikramarkudu is the film that confirmed Ravi Teja as a commercially bankable lead in Telugu commercial cinema — an action-comedy built around the actor's specific gifts for physical comedy and mass hero energy simultaneously. The film was remade in multiple languages, confirming the universality of its basic premise: a tough cop who must pretend to be a coward.

2006.title: Sivaji: The Boss
2006.note: Shankar's Sivaji: The Boss is Tamil cinema's most expensive and most maximalist film to that point — a production that understood spectacle as a political statement about what Tamil cinema was capable of achieving. Rajinikanth's presence absorbs everything Shankar throws at it: the colour, the choreography, the heroic excess. The film's commercial dominance across Tamil Nadu and among the diaspora was not a surprise; the scale of it was.

2006.title: Sillunu Oru Kadhal
2006.note: Vikram K. Kumar's Sillunu Oru Kadhal is a Tamil romantic film built around A.R. Rahman's score to an unusual degree — the music does not accompany the emotion but generates it, and the film's visual and narrative choices are consistently organised around what the songs need rather than the reverse. Suriya, Jyothika and Bhumika Chawla create a genuine triangle in which all three positions earn sympathy.

2006.title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest

2007.title: Om Shanti Om
2007.note: Farah Khan's Om Shanti Om is Hindi cinema's most joyful meta-text — a film about Bollywood that uses Bollywood's entire vocabulary to simultaneously celebrate and excavate it. Shah Rukh Khan playing a junior artiste who becomes a superstar across two lifetimes is the most self-aware career statement a Hindi film star has made. The climactic sequence, which assembles nearly every significant Bollywood star of the era in the same frame, is an act of industry solidarity disguised as entertainment.

2007.title: Chak De! India
2007.note: Shimit Amin's Chak De! India is the finest sports film in Hindi cinema — a narrative about the Indian women's hockey team that uses the sport to interrogate gender, regional identity and institutional masculinity simultaneously. Shah Rukh Khan's Coach Kabir Khan operates entirely in restraint, never asking the camera for the kind of romantic approval it usually grants him. The film's climactic match is as well-directed a sporting sequence as Indian cinema has produced.

2007.title: Bheja Fry
2007.note: Sagar Bellary's Bheja Fry is the most surprising Hindi commercial success of 2007 — a low-budget adaptation of the French film Le Dîner de Cons that cost almost nothing and returned several multiples of its investment through pure word-of-mouth. Vinay Pathak's Bharat Bhushan, the annoying guest who dismantles a sophisticated host's evening, is one of the decade's most complete comic performances. The film's success demonstrated that content could still find an audience without conventional marketing infrastructure.

2007.title: Welcome
2007.note: Anees Bazmee's Welcome is the most commercially efficient Bollywood comedy of 2007 — a star-assembled farce that paired Akshay Kumar's reactive timing against Anil Kapoor and Nana Patekar's anarchic energy, creating a comic dynamic that generated more from the collision of styles than from any individual moment. The film's complete comfort with its own absurdity gave it a lightness that audiences found irresistible at scale.

2007.title: Saawariya
2007.note: Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Saawariya was the most anticipated and most disappointing Hindi film of 2007 — a debut vehicle for Ranbir Kapoor and Sonam Kapoor that buried its leads in a production design so overwhelming it became unclear whether the humans were inhabiting the film or decorating it. The film's monochrome palette and operatic staging were formally interesting; its emotional register was somehow cold despite the surface heat. Ranbir Kapoor's charm survived the film's failure; Bhansali's sensibility did not adapt to it.

2007.title: Partner
2007.note: David Dhawan's Partner is Salman Khan at his most purely commercial — a man who understood exactly what his audience wanted and delivered it with a generosity that rewarded their fidelity. Govinda's return to mainstream commercial cinema gave the film an additional charge: two performers who operate in the same register competing to outdo each other. The film's ₹72 Cr collection in 2007 confirmed Salman's commercial rehabilitation after a difficult mid-2000s period.

2007.title: Yamadonga
2007.note: S.S. Rajamouli's Yamadonga is a Telugu fantasy film about a thief who travels to the afterlife — a conceptually unusual commercial film that allowed Rajamouli to work at scale without the historical epic framework. Jr NTR's dual performance and the film's production design ambition demonstrate Rajamouli extending his visual vocabulary into fantasy territory that would eventually inform Baahubali's mythological grammar.

2007.title: Polladhavan
2007.note: Vetrimaaran's Polladhavan is a Tamil revenge thriller about a young man whose motorcycle is stolen — an absurdly modest premise that the film treats with the moral seriousness of a Greek tragedy. Dhanush's performance is the film's discovery: a complete emotional honesty that subsequent Tamil films would ask of him repeatedly. The film launched both a director and a star in the same frame.

2007.title: Dasavathaaram
2007.note: Shankar's Dasavathaaram is Tamil cinema's most technically ambitious film to that point — Kamal Haasan in ten different roles, ranging from a 12th-century Vaishnava saint to a contemporary bioterrorism plot, held together by the film's conviction that history rhymes. The ten-role premise generates more admiration for the prosthetics than for the narrative coherence, but as a demonstration of what was technically possible in Tamil cinema, it remained unmatched for years.

2007.title: Rajamanikyam
2007.note: Vyshakh's Rajamanikyam gave Mammootty one of his most commercially successful action roles of the decade — a film that understood what the star's mature presence could do with a mass entertainment framework. The film's Kerala action-comedy register is distinctive from both Tamil and Hindi commercial cinema, and its commercial performance confirmed Mammootty's sustained relevance across demographic groups.

2007.title: Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
Transformers
2007.note: Michael Bay's Transformers was the introduction of the modern American CGI blockbuster to the Indian multiplex audience at scale — a film whose spectacle was entirely mediated by digital effects and whose emotional content was almost entirely secondary to the experience of watching machines transform. The film's India gross marked the beginning of a sustained Hollywood-India multiplex relationship that would grow significantly across the following decade.

2008.title: Ghajini
2008.note: A.R. Murugadoss's Ghajini gave Aamir Khan his most physically transformed performance — 25 kg of muscle added for the role — and the anterograde amnesia premise gave the revenge narrative an unusual structural logic. The film's ₹200 Cr collection made it the first Hindi film to cross that threshold, a record that remained for two years. Its commercial significance was architectural: it established that Hindi films could operate at a scale previously only achieved by South Indian productions.

2008.title: Jodhaa Akbar
2008.note: Ashutosh Gowariker's Jodhaa Akbar is the most expensive and most aesthetically accomplished historical epic in Hindi cinema — a three-hour reconstruction of the Mughal court that treated spectacle as a form of argument about tolerance. Hrithik Roshan's Akbar and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's Jodha generate a romantic chemistry that the film's formal grandeur somehow intensifies rather than overwhelms. A.R. Rahman's score is among his most compositionally ambitious.

2008.title: Singh Is Kinng
2008.note: Anees Bazmee's Singh Is Kinng is pure Akshay Kumar commercial cinema in its most distilled form — a film that asks nothing of its audience beyond enjoyment and delivers it consistently for two hours. Katrina Kaif's visual presence and Akshay's Sikh-honour comedy provided the elements that the decade's commercial entertainment required. The film's ₹80 Cr collection confirmed that Akshay was operating at the top tier of Hindi commercial performers.

2008.title: Dostana
2008.note: Tarun Mansukhani's Dostana is Hindi cinema's most commercially successful engagement with gay identity — a film that uses homosexuality as comic premise while being more affectionate about it than its detractors acknowledged. John Abraham, Abhishek Bachchan and Priyanka Chopra generate a triangle whose comedy depends on mutual affection as much as misunderstanding. The film's commercial success demonstrated that urban Indian audiences were ready for this conversation even if the film itself wasn't ready to have it fully.

2008.title: Rock On!!
2008.note: Abhishek Kapoor's Rock On!! is the film that made guitar-playing middle-class men feel that their lives were dramatic enough to be the subject of Hindi cinema. Farhan Akhtar's performance as the reluctant rock star anchors a film that treats the compromises of adulthood as genuinely tragic rather than simply inevitable. The film's cult following grew steadily after its theatrical run, sustained by people who recognised themselves in its portrait of abandoned dreams.

2008.title: Race
2008.note: Abbas-Mustan's Race is the most accomplished Hindi thriller of the decade's second half — a film of such sustained narrative unreliability that even on second viewing its reveals feel surprising. Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Khanna's fraternal antagonism drives a plot whose reversals are genuine rather than merely mechanical. Pritam's score gave the film a specific nightlife aesthetic that its characters inhabit completely.

2008.title: Jalsa
2008.note: Trivikram Srinivas's Jalsa is the film that confirmed Pawan Kalyan's status as Telugu cinema's most mass-affecting star — a film whose theatrical scenes generated audience responses that contemporary accounts describe as closer to religious celebration than entertainment. The story is conventional Telugu action drama; what is unconventional is the intensity of audience identification with the lead. The film's ₹65 Cr collection was the highest for a Pawan Kalyan film to that point.

2008.title: The Dark Knight
2008.note: Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight found its Indian audience through the same mechanism as most successful Hollywood films in India — word of mouth from urban multiplexes extending to the broader audience through the week. Heath Ledger's Joker operates in a register of comic villainy that translated without friction: the anarchist who has no plan is a universally recognisable threat. The film's India gross was modest by Hollywood standards; its cultural impact — in design, in meme culture, in subsequent villain performances — was large.

2008.title: Iron Man
2008.note: Jon Favreau's Iron Man was the foundational film of a franchise universe that would become the defining Hollywood commercial phenomenon of the following decade — but in 2008 it was simply a very good superhero film with a charismatic lead. Robert Downey Jr's Tony Stark found immediate recognition in Indian audiences accustomed to the billionaire hero who uses technology and wit rather than supernatural powers. The India gross reflected enthusiastic multiplex uptake.

2008.title: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull

2009.title: 3 Idiots
2009.note: Rajkumar Hirani's 3 Idiots is the most watched Hindi film in history by some metrics — a comedy about engineering education and the pressure it generates that somehow managed to be simultaneously the funniest and most emotionally devastating film of 2009. Aamir Khan's Rancho, Sharman Joshi's Raju and R. Madhavan's Farhan are the decade's most complete ensemble, three performers who make the film's thesis about following passion feel like personal advice rather than screenwriting. 'All izz well' entered the cultural language as a genuine coping mechanism.

2009.title: Love Aaj Kal
2009.note: Imtiaz Ali's Love Aaj Kal is an Ali film about the way that time and distance and modernity complicate love — a double timeline that compares a 1965 romance's directness with a 2009 relationship's ambivalence. Saif Ali Khan and Deepika Padukone's contemporary story generates the film's commercial appeal; the 1965 story, with Rishi Kapoor's cameo as the aged narrator, carries its emotional weight. The film confirmed Deepika Padukone as a leading presence the industry needed to think about.

2009.title: Ajab Prem Ki Ghazab Kahani
2009.note: Rajkumar Santoshi's Ajab Prem Ki Ghazab Kahani is Ranbir Kapoor and Katrina Kaif at their most commercially buoyant — a comedy that plays entirely to their strengths without asking anything from either that they couldn't deliver. The film's Manali setting and its cheerful narrative incompetence gave it an accidental charm that more constructed films of the era couldn't manufacture. Among the most rewatchable mainstream comedies of 2009.

2009.title: Wanted
2009.note: Prabhu Deva's Wanted is Salman Khan's commercial resurrection — a mass action film that abandoned every pretension to realistic psychology and delivered the Khan persona in its most concentrated, weaponised form. The film's action sequences are choreographed with a Telugu commercial cinema energy that Bollywood had been importing selectively and which here found its most commercially successful Hindi context. Salman's single-dialogue delivery in this film launched a career phase that has not ended.

2009.title: Kaminey
2009.note: Vishal Bhardwaj's Kaminey is the most formally ambitious mainstream Hindi film of 2009 — a twin-brothers crime thriller set in Mumbai's underworld that uses the doppelganger premise to examine complicity, chance and the porousness of moral identity. Shahid Kapoor's double performance, one character with a stammer and one with a lisp, is a technical achievement that the film's critical reputation has perhaps insufficiently acknowledged. Bhardwaj's visual grammar for Mumbai crime is as distinct as anything in contemporary Hindi cinema.

2009.title: New York
2009.note: Kabir Khan's New York is a post-9/11 thriller about three Indian students and the surveillance state they find themselves navigating — a subject that allowed Hindi cinema to engage with the War on Terror's human cost in ways that its domestic politics rarely permitted. John Abraham, Neil Nitin Mukesh and Katrina Kaif form a triangle whose chemistry the thriller's mechanics make genuinely consequential. Salim-Sulaiman's score is among the better works of their collaborative period.

2009.title: Paa
2009.note: R. Balki's Paa cast Amitabh Bachchan as a 12-year-old boy with progeria and Abhishek Bachchan as his father — an inversion of their real relationship that the film uses as both gimmick and genuine dramatic conceit. Bachchan's physical transformation is total and his performance within it surprisingly unshowy, which is the correct choice for a character whose disability is neither pitied nor diminished. A film that required courage from its makers and found it.

2009.title: Dev D
2009.note: Anurag Kashyap's Dev D is the most radical rethinking of Sharat Chandra's Devdas — an adaptation that takes the self-destructive romantic and makes him answerable for his self-destruction rather than pathetic because of it. Abhay Deol's contemporary Dev is petty, selfish and occasionally funny, which is a more honest portrait of the original character than most versions permit. Amit Trivedi's score, mixing electronica with folk, created a sonic texture that was genuinely new to Hindi cinema.

2009.title: Magadheera
2009.note: S.S. Rajamouli's Magadheera was the film that made pan-India cinema a viable commercial category before the term was coined — a Telugu production whose VFX budget and historical-fantasy scope were previously reserved for Hollywood, finding audiences across every Indian language market. Ram Charan's dual role, the period warrior and his reincarnated present-day descendant, gave Rajamouli the temporal frame he would later expand to its logical extreme in Baahubali. The film's ₹115 Cr collection is the decade's most significant Telugu commercial milestone.

2009.title: Aarya 2
2009.note: Sukumar's Aarya 2 is the sequel that surpassed its original — a second chapter of the obsessive lover story that gave Allu Arjun his most commercially successful early film. The film's portrayal of romantic fixation is more complex than conventional Telugu romance, and Allu Arjun's physical expressiveness gave the character a specificity that would define his acting identity for years before Pushpa revised it.

2009.title: Ayan
2009.note: K.V. Anand's Ayan is a Tamil action film that gave Suriya a commercial vehicle built around his physical capabilities and international production values. The film's gun-running plot gave it a global geography — Malaysia, Bangkok, South Africa — that Tamil commercial cinema was beginning to explore as production budgets expanded. Harris Jayaraj's score maintained the sound he had established across Tamil romantic action cinema.

2009.title: Avatar
2009.note: James Cameron's Avatar was Indian cinema's first real encounter with RealD 3D, and the theatrical experience — the specific sensation of a world built around immersive technology — drove repeat viewings at a scale that had not been seen since the 1990s. The film's India gross of ₹45 Cr was at that point the highest for a Hollywood film in the market and demonstrated that the Indian multiplex infrastructure had reached a point where global event cinema could find its full audience. The Na'vi planet's visual grammar influenced Indian period epic design for years.

2009.title: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian

1951.title: Awaara
1951.note: Awaara became one of the most watched Indian films internationally before 'international' was a concept Indian cinema dared to aim for — it ran for years in the Soviet Union, Middle East and China, with Russian audiences reportedly singing its songs in the streets. Raj Kapoor's Chaplinesque tramp was not just a character but a political statement about class, aspiration and the new Indian republic. The film's emotional architecture — can a man born to crime become good? — is still the question Indian cinema returns to every decade.

1955.title: Shree 420
1955.note: Shree 420 gave Hindi cinema its most durable anthem — 'Mera Joota Hai Japani' became the signature song of newly independent India's complicated relationship with modernity, patriotism and the temptations of the city. Raj Kapoor understood that the migrant's journey from village to Bombay was the defining story of post-Partition India, and he told it with a lightness that made the sadness bearable. The film is essentially a moral fable dressed as a musical, and it holds its shape better than most films from any era.

1957.title: Mother India
1957.note: Mother India is the film India submitted to the Oscars and it nearly won — losing Best Foreign Film by a single vote, one of the closest margins in Academy history. Nargis's Radha is not just a character but a civilisational argument: that suffering is ennobling, that the land is sacred, that a mother's love for her son can coexist with her duty to execute him. No Hindi film before or since has carried that weight with such moral seriousness.

1957.title: Pyaasa
1957.cast: Guru Dutt, Waheeda Rehman, Mala Sinha
1957.note: Time Out magazine listed Pyaasa among the 100 greatest films ever made — it is the only Hindi film on that list, and it belongs there. Guru Dutt's portrait of a poet rejected by a society that only values him once it thinks he is dead is among the most formally accomplished things Indian cinema produced in the 20th century. S.D. Burman's score and Sahir Ludhianvi's lyrics operate at a level of artistic integration that most films never approach.

1960.title: Mughal-e-Azam
1960.note: Mughal-e-Azam took 16 years to make, bankrupted its producers twice, and still became the highest-grossing Indian film of its era — a record it held for over a decade. K. Asif's obsessive attention to period authenticity meant genuine Mughal artefacts, 2,000 real soldiers in battle sequences, and costumes of actual silk and zardozi. The film's 2004 colourised re-release became a box office event, proving that certain films transcend the era they were made in entirely.

1964.title: Sangam
1964.note: Sangam was the first Indian film to be shot extensively in Europe, and its travelogue sequences in Paris, Switzerland and Rome essentially invented the aspirational overseas fantasy that would define Hindi cinema's visual vocabulary for thirty years. Raj Kapoor understood that Indian audiences wanted to see India in foreign landscapes, not just romance — and he gave them both. At three hours and forty minutes, Sangam was also the longest hit of its era, evidence that audiences would follow a story anywhere if they trusted the filmmaker.

1965.title: Guide
1965.note: Guide is one of the most psychologically complex films Hindi cinema produced in the 1960s — Raju's transformation from tourist guide to con-man to accidental spiritual leader is not a redemption arc but an honest portrait of how identity is performed under pressure. Based on R.K. Narayan's novel, it asked whether a man can become what others need him to be even if he never believes it himself. S.D. Burman's score remains among the finest in Indian film history.

1969.title: Aradhana
1969.note: Aradhana is the film that made Rajesh Khanna a phenomenon so large that women reportedly sent him letters in blood and married his photograph — a level of stardom Indian cinema had never seen and has arguably never seen since. Kishore Kumar's voice became inseparable from Khanna's screen presence from this film onward, a partnership that defined an era. The film's climactic revelation in a courtroom is one of Hindi cinema's great melodramatic constructions.

1971.title: Haathi Mere Saathi
1971.note: Haathi Mere Saathi ran for over a year in many theatres and cemented Rajesh Khanna's status as Hindi cinema's first true superstar — a man for whom entire audiences returned week after week. The film's central conceit, a man who chooses his elephants over his wife, sounds absurd summarised; in execution it is a film about loyalty, innocence and the cruelty of society toward those who love differently. Laxmikant-Pyarelal's score remains immediately recognisable fifty years later.

1971.title: Anand
1971.note: Anand is the film that introduced Amitabh Bachchan as a serious dramatic presence and gave Rajesh Khanna his finest performance — the two stars working in the same frame is one of those accidents of casting that retrospectively feels inevitable. Hrishikesh Mukherjee's restraint as a director is what makes the film's emotional power so cumulative: he never telegraphs what is coming, which means when it arrives it is genuinely devastating. 'Babumoshai, zindagi badi honi chahiye, lambi nahi' is still quoted at funerals.

1973.title: Zanjeer
1973.note: Zanjeer was rejected by every major star of the era — Dharmendra, Dev Anand, Rajesh Khanna all passed — before Prakash Mehra cast an unknown Amitabh Bachchan, and the rest is the most documented turning point in Hindi cinema history. The Angry Young Man was born here: a police inspector who operates outside the system because the system cannot deliver justice, a character so precisely timed to post-Emergency India that it felt less like fiction and more like a national confession. Salim-Javed's screenplay remains a masterclass in channelling social frustration into popular entertainment.

1973.title: Bobby
1973.note: Bobby launched two careers simultaneously — Rishi Kapoor's as a leading man and Dimple Kapadia's as a screen presence — and became the definitive Indian teenager movie, a genre Hindi cinema had barely acknowledged existed before 1973. Raj Kapoor understood youth culture intuitively: the two-piece swimsuit, the motorcycle, the defiance of class boundaries were not provocations but accurate observations. The film's commercial success reoriented Bollywood toward a younger demographic that would define the industry for the next decade.

1975.title: Sholay
1975.cast: Amitabh Bachchan, Dharmendra, Hema Malini, Jaya Bhaduri, Sanjeev Kumar, Amjad Khan
1975.note: Sholay ran for five years at Mumbai's Minerva cinema and is still the benchmark against which every Indian blockbuster is privately measured — not just commercially but cinematically. Gabbar Singh is the most quoted villain in the history of Indian film, which is remarkable given that he appears on screen for less than fifteen minutes; Amjad Khan's performance is so complete that the absence of Gabbar creates as much dread as his presence. Salim-Javed's screenplay is the closest thing Indian popular cinema has produced to a perfect genre construction.

1975.title: Deewaar
1975.cast: Amitabh Bachchan, Shashi Kapoor, Nirupa Roy
1975.note: Released the same year as Sholay, Deewaar made 1975 the single most important year in Hindi cinema's commercial history — two films from two different directors establishing the template for action cinema that Indian filmmakers are still following. Salim-Javed's script posed a question the audience was genuinely uncertain about: which brother is right? The most famous four words in Hindi cinema — 'Mere paas maa hai' — were improvised on set by Shashi Kapoor and are now permanently inscribed in the language.

1975.title: Jai Santoshi Maa
1975.note: Jai Santoshi Maa is one of Hindi cinema's most counterintuitive blockbusters — a devotional film made on minimal budget that outgrossed virtually every mainstream release of 1975 by building an audience Bollywood had entirely overlooked. Women in small towns and rural India watched it as a religious act, bringing offerings to the cinema hall and conducting the film's prescribed fast — a participatory experience that no mainstream film had engineered. It remains one of the clearest examples of Indian cinema's unique capacity to serve simultaneously as popular entertainment and spiritual practice.

1977.title: Amar Akbar Anthony
1977.cast: Amitabh Bachchan, Vinod Khanna, Rishi Kapoor, Shabana Azmi
1977.note: Manmohan Desai's secular vision of India — three brothers separated at birth, raised Hindu, Muslim and Christian, reunited by love and coincidence — was a commercial argument for pluralism at a time when the Emergency had fractured the national conversation. Amar Akbar Anthony is deliberately, almost programmatically absurd, and that absurdism is its political intelligence: the film knows that no realistic film could make this argument without being dismissed. Amitabh's Anthony Gonsalves — drunk, loyal, funny — is one of the great comic performances in Hindi cinema.

1978.title: Don
1978.note: Don gave Amitabh Bachchan his most technically demanding role — playing both a suave underworld don and his innocent double simultaneously — and the film's central reveal remains one of Hindi cinema's most rewatchable twists. The Kalyanji-Anandji score, particularly the title song, is the audio equivalent of a neon sign: impossible to ignore, immediately evocative of an entire aesthetic era. Farhan Akhtar's 2006 remake is the sincerest possible tribute, though it wisely declined to compete with the original's effortless cool.

1978.title: Muqaddar Ka Sikandar
1978.note: Muqaddar Ka Sikandar is the film that established Amitabh Bachchan's template for the tragic hero — a man whose love is never returned, whose friendship is betrayed, whose sacrifice is witnessed only by the audience. Kishore Kumar singing 'Rote Hue Aate Hain Sab' over the opening credits is among the most emotionally pre-loaded beginnings in Hindi cinema: you know before the story starts that this man will suffer. The film was the second-highest grossing Hindi film of 1978 despite competing with Bachchan's own Don — a feat that illustrates just how dominant he was at that moment.

1979.title: Suhaag
1979.note: Suhaag belongs to the peak of Manmohan Desai's masala universe — a film so structurally confident in its own excess that it never apologises for a single coincidence or contrivance. The lost brothers formula that Desai had refined across a decade here reaches a kind of terminal velocity, where every plot mechanism arrives precisely when needed and the audience's job is simply to feel what the film instructs them to feel. Amitabh Bachchan's screen presence by 1979 had become so total that Desai simply built the architecture of the film around it.

1980.title: Shaan
1980.cast: Amitabh Bachchan, Shashi Kapoor, Sunil Dutt
1980.note: Ramesh Sippy followed Sholay with Shaan — an openly Bond-influenced action spectacle that was Bollywood's most ambitious technical production of its era, with underwater sequences, helicopter chases and a villain's island lair that had never been attempted in Indian cinema before. The film underperformed relative to expectations precisely because Sholay had set an impossible standard, but evaluated on its own terms Shaan is a technically accomplished film that rewired how Indian action films thought about production design. Kulbhushan Kharbanda's villain Shakaal became a template for the suave, English-speaking antagonist.

1981.title: Silsila
1981.note: Silsila's commercial performance was considered a disappointment at the time, which is fascinating given that it has been watched and discussed continuously for over four decades. The off-screen relationship between Bachchan, Rekha and Jaya Bhaduri transformed what would have been a conventional love triangle into something audiences experienced as documentary — the sensation that the film was true even if it never confirmed it. Yash Chopra's visual language for romantic yearning, all mustard fields and Swiss mountains, is at its most precise here.

1982.title: Shakti
1982.cast: Dilip Kumar, Amitabh Bachchan, Smita Patil
1982.note: Shakti is the only film where Dilip Kumar and Amitabh Bachchan shared the screen as equals — the acknowledged greatest actor of the previous generation against the defining star of the present one — and the tension between their performance styles is the film's engine. Ramesh Sippy structured the narrative around their incompatibility: a father who chose duty over his son, a son who could never forgive him. Film students still watch the scene where they argue across a table as an exercise in how two completely different acting philosophies can create genuine electricity.

1983.title: Coolie
1983.cast: Amitabh Bachchan, Rishi Kapoor, Waheeda Rehman
1983.note: Coolie holds a unique place in Hindi cinema history because the near-fatal on-set accident that hospitalised Amitabh Bachchan during production became the biggest news story in India for weeks — and when he recovered, the film's release was treated as a national celebration. Manmohan Desai deliberately retained the frame of Bachchan getting punched in the stomach, making the real accident visible in the theatrical print, which audiences watched with the knowledge that they were seeing the moment their hero nearly died. The film's box office was driven as much by relief as by entertainment.

1983.title: Hero
1983.note: Hero launched Jackie Shroff from nowhere — an almost entirely unknown actor who became a star on the strength of a single film because Subhash Ghai understood that a new kind of hero was possible. Less angry than Bachchan, more physical than Dharmendra, Shroff's Raju offered the 1980s a leading man who could be both a rebel and a romantic simultaneously. Laxmikant-Pyarelal's 'Tu Mera Jaanu Hai' remains one of the decade's most distinctive musical moments.

1983.title: Betaab
1983.note: Betaab introduced Sunny Deol and Amrita Singh in the same frame and created one of the decade's most watched debut pairings — both newcomers who looked like they had always belonged on screen together. The film's Pahalgam locations gave Hindi romantic cinema its most consistently beautiful visual backdrop of the decade, and every subsequent romance that filmed in Kashmir owed Betaab a debt. Rahul Dev Burman's score is gentle where the era's action films were relentless, which made it feel genuinely different.

1984.title: Sharaabi
1984.note: Sharaabi gave Amitabh Bachchan his most deliberately comic role of the decade while somehow remaining emotionally credible — the drunk millionaire who is simultaneously ridiculous and pitiable is a difficult tonal balance that Bachchan manages through sheer specificity of performance. Kishore Kumar's songs, particularly 'Manzilein Apni Jagah Hain', carry a weariness that operates underneath the film's surface comedy. The film is essentially a character study wearing the costume of a commercial entertainer.

1986.title: Nagina
1986.note: Nagina is the film that established Sridevi as the dominant female star of 1980s Hindi cinema — not as a romantic lead but as the protagonist of a supernatural thriller in which she carries almost every scene alone. The snake-woman premise gave her permission to be physically expressive, terrifying and seductive in ways that the conventional romantic heroine role did not allow, and she took that permission and built something indelible. Laxmikant-Pyarelal's 'Main Teri Dushman' became one of the decade's most iconic musical sequences.

1986.title: Karma
1986.cast: Dilip Kumar, Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff, Sridevi
1986.note: Karma assembled four of the biggest stars of two different generations — Dilip Kumar representing old Bollywood, Anil Kapoor and Jackie Shroff the new — and Subhash Ghai managed the ensemble with the confidence of a filmmaker who understood that star presence is itself a kind of storytelling. The film's anti-terrorism plot was a direct response to the political violence of the mid-1980s, and Indian audiences responded to the catharsis. At ₹9 Cr it was among the biggest grossers of 1986, making it Ghai's commercial peak to that point.

1987.title: Mr. India
1987.note: Mr. India is the rare Indian superhero film that does not feel embarrassed by its own premise — Shekhar Kapur treats invisibility as a genuine dramatic device rather than a special-effects showcase, which is what elevates it above the decade's other fantasy films. Amrish Puri's Mogambo is the villain that defined a generation's understanding of cinematic evil: operatically dressed, grandiosely spoken, utterly committed to the bit. Sridevi's Charlie Chaplin sequence is so complete as a piece of physical comedy that it would be remarkable in any language film.

1988.title: Tezaab
1988.note: Tezaab launched Madhuri Dixit into a stardom that would define the next decade — 'Ek Do Teen' is one of the most viscerally entertaining song sequences in Hindi cinema, and its success was built entirely on her ability to make disciplined choreography look like pure spontaneous joy. The film itself is a revenge thriller with a genuinely dark undertow that the musical sequences only partially soften: N. Chandra understood that the 1980s audience wanted both catharsis and sensation. At ₹13 Cr it was the highest-grossing Hindi film of 1988.

1989.title: Maine Pyar Kiya
1989.note: Maine Pyar Kiya is one of those films that arrives so precisely timed to a cultural mood that it seems less like it was made and more like it was discovered — the wholesome romance, the family values, the pigeon that carries letters, all felt simultaneously innocent and new after a decade of action cinema. Salman Khan's debut established a kind of uncomplicated masculinity that was different from Bachchan's tormented anger and Khanna's melancholy, and the audience responded with the largest box office numbers of the decade. Sooraj Barjatya never made a film that didn't make money; this one explained why.

1989.title: Ram Lakhan
1989.cast: Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff, Madhuri Dixit
1989.note: Ram Lakhan is Subhash Ghai at his most maximalist — every scene is larger than it needs to be, every performance pushed to the edge of what the frame can hold, and somehow it works because Ghai understood that masala cinema is a form of opera. The two-brother structure gave Anil Kapoor and Jackie Shroff complementary trajectories that played to their individual strengths: Kapoor's physical comedy versus Shroff's brooding intensity. Madhuri Dixit's Radha became the decade's most popular on-screen heroine.

1989.title: Chandni
1989.note: Chandni is Yash Chopra's love letter to a certain kind of femininity — radiant, independent, emotionally sovereign — and Sridevi inhabited it so completely that the film's palette of white and gold became her signature aesthetic. It was the film that shifted Chopra's grammar away from the tragic love stories of the 1970s toward a more optimistic romanticism, and that optimism would carry through all of his subsequent work including Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge. The Switzerland sequences are so visually consistent and beautiful that they function as a brand identity for Indian romantic cinema abroad.
